Uniform Title: Gorakṣayogaśāstram Secondary Title: Mūlasāra Author: Gorakṣanātha (attributed)
Manuscript: NGMCP 5-332; Reel Number: B24/44

Description: *Gorakṣayogaśāstram*, also known as *Mūlasāra* (The Essence of the Root), is a work on Yoga composed in the form of a *stotra* (hymn). By reading and reciting it daily, one acquires immeasurable benefits. It begins with a summary of the contents of the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*), including the vital channels (*nāḍīs*), the sun, moon, and fire, the *cakras*, the sacred *kaula* sites, the self (*ātman*) residing therein, the fourteen worlds, the oceans, and the rivers—indeed, everything contained within the cosmic egg of Brahmā (*brahmāṇḍa*) exists within the body. It describes how the moon upon the summit of the internal Mount Meru pours down nectar throughout the body, thus detailing the activities and functions of the internal constituents of the body enumerated at the outset. As its very name indicates, this treatise (*śāstra*) is attributed to Gorakṣanātha, the founder of Haṭhayoga.
Notes: December 17, 2013. Country of Publication: India.
Homage to Ādinātha!
The Lord said:
The moon, the sun, and likewise fire; the ten channels within the body; the five stationary vital airs, and likewise the mind and the bindu. (1)
The six cakras and the spinal column (merudaṇḍa), as well as Oḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, and Śrīhastaka. ||2||
Prakīrti, Kṣetrapuruṣa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; likewise the rivers, streams, oceans, and the fourteen worlds. ||3||
Whatever qualities exist in the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa) reside within the physical body; O Śubhismṛti, they declare that the goal is to achieve a concise mastery over them. ||4||
2a) Standing on the peak of Meru, the moon, joined by sixteen digits,
facing downward, pours down nectar day and night with the brilliance of frost. (5)
Śudhāṃśu, dhi, viṣaśrāvī, and pīyūṣabiṃdu are [names of meters]; tarala is to be known as śudha, while ghana is declared to be biṃdu. ||6||
The single dot (bindu) is eternally Brahmā, the savior of creation and preservation;
through the mastery of the group of dots, the perfection of the body is produced.
Resembling a hibiscus flower, situated in the beautiful region of the pubic bone and pervading the base of the middle channel, the Sun resides within embodied beings. 8.
2b) The sun consists of twelve *kalās*, while fire is endowed with ten *kalās*;
the digestive fire (*pāvaka*) that consumes food and so forth always resides within all embodied beings. 9.
The moon rains down frost, while the sun always blazes intensely;
when the vital breath (prāṇa) remains in conjunction with them, death occurs through their separation. ||10||
The wise knowers of Yoga understand that through practice, one who can assume any form at will attains union with the rays of the sun above and the nectar of the moon below. 11.
O Goddess, this is proclaimed as dwelling in the ocean of yoga; and by means of the single union of prāṇa and apāna, one becomes free from disease. 12.
The prāṇa is to be known as consisting of the moon, and likewise the apāna consists of the sun;
the union of these two is the means for accomplishing the seed-syllable of passion (rajas). 13.

Having firmly performed the *oḍḍīyāna-bandha* and the exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*), there is the union of the *samāna* and *apāna* winds through the single integration of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*. (14)
In Kāmarūpa, there is the triple union of prāṇa, apāna, and samāna;
the power (śakti) at the navel between these two is called Oḍḍiyāna. ||15||
Jālandhara is to be known in the fire [cakra], and Kāmarūpa in the womb [cakra];
Pūrṇagiri is in the heart, Śrīhāṭaka is in the middle, and Oḍḍiyāna is above the palate. (16)
Having contracted the root of the tongue and placed the chin upon the heart,
having restrained the nine gates and filled the belly with air— 18.
The movement [of breath] through all the channels causes the fire of the body to blaze;
from the constant blazing of that fire, the digestion of food and other substances occurs. (19)

Through the constant digestion of food and other substances, an increase of the vital essence (*rasa*) arises; by its very nature, this occurs within the seed itself as it sustains the *bindu*, and not otherwise. (19)
They exist in all limbs in eightfold ways;
indeed, it is the wind alone that is proclaimed as the supreme root-essence within the body. (20)
O God, through the purification of the vital air (vāyu), there is an increase in lifespan day by day.
Prāṇa resides in the heart, apāna in the rectum, and samāna is situated in the navel.
4a) Udāna is located in the region of the throat, and vyāna pervades the entire body; having withdrawn the local winds again and again into the region of the pelvic bones. (22)
At the moment of the upward stroke (udghāta), the wind, having passed through the well-guarded wheel-shaft of the Suṣumṇā and then transcending the Brahma-knot, enters the Madhyamā.
Then the wind enters the svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra at the base of the liṅga;
thereafter, one should always perceive its movement reaching the maṇipūra at the region of the navel. (24)
Having pierced the Viṣṇu-knot in the center of the heart and the source of qualities at the throat,
one should pierce the root of the palate in the nectar-wheel and proceed to the abode of Rudra.
When the wind (cakra) moves through each city after having pierced the wheel (cakra), the drop (bindu) goes to that very place through its conjunction with the wind. ||26||
As long as it remains in the *yoni*, the wind moves from the station of the *bindu*;
having reached the stalk of the *śaṅkhinī*, it sustains the bone-void.
Then his body will certainly become composed of milk, perfected as a solid mass;
thus, through the practice of yoga, the man who is established in Brahman [attains this]. (28)
His sin, accumulated over hundreds of millions of births, goes to destruction;
and month after month, he shall obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha). ||29||
5a) O King Varṣaṇa, there is no doubt regarding the fruit of that [practice]:
all sins accumulated over ten million births are consumed by it. (30)
In this very world, through the yoga of practice, the muttering of mantras (japa), austerities, sacrifices, gifts, and vows are said to be like fire to grass. (31)
Through the power of repeated practice, those [merits] become multiplied by millions upon millions;
all the ancestors rejoice when a son follows the path of yoga.
And they enjoyed all happiness, free from every suffering. The Goddess said:
O Moon-crested Lord, tell me the means for the practice of yoga,
by attaining which all yogis are liberated from the bondage of birth. (5b) 33.
The Lord said:
Brahmā resides in the center of the navel, while Mādhava is in the center of the heart;
Śaṅkara is to be known as being in the head. This triad of locations is remembered as the bestower of liberation.
The supreme light, like a lamp, ten finger-breadths in extent, exists as a mass of radiance like a wheel in the center of the navel and in the middle of the heart.

One should meditate upon the light of Śiva at the crown of the head, resembling pure crystal, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons, and appearing like a mass of ghee extracted from clarified butter.
Having made the mind steady, the wise should gradually effect the union of the three lights with the wind and the bindu by means of the mind. (37)

In Kāmarūpa, within the channel of the wheel, one perceives the individual light in the central channel at the center of the field; likewise, in all the wheels, the individual light is clearly seen. (38)
In that [state] where, through practice, the vital air, the mind, and likewise the bindu—these three—reside within the light, there the Self is firmly established. (39)
Just as light shines within all the centers of the navel,
even there, in that very void of the bone, the movement of time flees away.
6b) Thus, the Buddha should always perform meditation with the intellect, consisting of light;
for the wind-drop (vāyu-bindu), which unites the lights, is the bestower of liberation. //41//

Thus, for one whose mind is steady in meditation and whose speech is not found [to distract] the mind—for such a person, the vital breath (vāyu), the drop (bindu), the mind, and the self (ātman) all become stable. (42)
When the *bindu* moves, when the consciousness moves, and when the vital air always moves, this moving one moves toward eternal death. (43)
Therefore, having become thus fickle,
[it] would come to be. ||44||
In the exposition of the yoga of meditation, when [the goal] has been forgotten, it is said:
"The Supreme Brahman, which transcends meditation, is hidden in all the scriptures. (45)
He alone is the all-pervading progenitor of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others;
he is the support of the worlds, abiding within the bodies of those who are themselves bodiless. 46.
7b) Pervading all, the Lord is devoid of qualities and beyond primordial nature;
the Self is free from birth, growth, and so forth, omnipresent and eternal. (47)
Having made the mind free from support, one should make the mind steady in the void;
one should destroy everything that is impermanent, whatever has been acquired by the mind. 48.
O Goddess, when the instruments [of action] and the mind itself, which are composed of the five elements and are constantly perishing, are led into Brahman, [then one is liberated]. (49)
Then, having attained the state of Brahman, the yogi shall proceed to the state of liberation;
for him, the powers such as atomization (*animā*) and the rest [shall manifest]. ||50||
8a) The Goddess said:
The Lord said: [Regarding] the faculties... [text fragment].
The cosmic egg is the supreme Brahman, auspicious and composed of light;
and above that is the supreme [abode] of Viṣṇu, endowed with qualities within his heart.
And above that, the realm of the Rudras is seen; there is no doubt about this.
And above that is the Great Void (Mahāśūnya), where Brahmā resides according to his station.
Having led the mind to that very place above, which consists of the Great Void, and knowing the protection of Time, one becomes oneself equal to Brahman. ||54||
8b) For this very reason, Pārvatī [remained] under the pretext of sleep while Śiva and the others were engaged in the contemplation of knowledge; nothing else could have occurred. //55//
In this way, Śakra and the other gods, as well as the Siddhas of excellent complexion, perform what is to be accomplished; they attain the supreme goal. ||56||
Within this body there are humans, gandharvas, uragas, and kinnaras;
having thus accomplished yoga, they go to the supreme destination. //57//
9a) One should avoid spending time with those intent on violence, thieves, atheists, speakers of untruth, the deceitful, the cruel, and those who revile the twice-born and the Vedas. //58//
Those who do not serve at the feet of the guru, who have abandoned all dharmas, who are afflicted by laziness, and those who are tormented by desire and anger; ||59||
Likewise, those devoid of practice fall away from yoga;
by that [practice], O Pārvatī, one attains the state of liberation through dharma, and not by this [mere theory].
9b) Some maintain that meditative absorption (dhyāna) and consciousness (vijñāna) are mutually successive. //61//
And those who, through instruction, possess knowledge regarding the duties of the Dharma and so forth, and having performed the practices in their proper sequence, they go to the supreme goal. ||62||
Whoever should constantly hear this narrative exactly as it has been remembered,
for him all sins shall perish, and he shall attain the abode of Brahmā.
Merely by hearing [this] once, one removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
on a single day, one obtains the fruit of horse-sacrifices.
Whoever recites this or causes it to be recited shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices;
there is no scripture more meritorious than this to be found anywhere. (65)
Thus ends the Gorakṣayogaśāstra, known as the Mūlasāra.
